claims.text: Rapid solidification produces nanoscale Mn2O3 precipitates in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
Nanoscale oxide precipitates enhance magnetoelastic coupling.
Nanoscale oxide precipitates pin magnetic domain walls.
The oxide precipitates govern a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields.
The oxide precipitates promote rapid heat exchange.
The oxide precipitates promote low magnetic hysteresis.
The oxide precipitates promote robust mechanical stability.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is a rare-earth-free high-entropy alloy.
Processed equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi naturally has a fine-grained matrix containing nanoscale Mn2O3 precipitates.
Changing cooling rate or making small compositional adjustments can control the volume fraction and size of nanoscale oxide precipitates.
The nanoscale Mn2O3 precipitates are located at cell or grain boundaries.
Localized domain-wall pinning by the precipitates facilitates rapid magnetic-moment reorientation at low fields.
Precipitate interfaces promote efficient heat transfer.
The precipitates mechanically strengthen the alloy.
Precipitate-induced strengthening reduces hysteresis during cyclic magnetization.
Increasing precipitate density or optimizing precipitate size will increase the low-field isothermal magnetic entropy change relative to a lower-density baseline.
Increasing precipitate density or optimizing precipitate size will lower magnetic hysteresis relative to the baseline.
Increasing precipitate density or optimizing precipitate size will maintain mechanical stability relative to the baseline.
SLM-processed equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi can exhibit high room-temperature yield strength and retain comparatively high strength through 700 degrees Celsius.

The proposed relationships should hold near room temperature, at low applied fields, for similar high-entropy-alloy compositions that have not undergone recrystallization or drastic precipitate-phase or size changes.

contradictions.description: The mechanism invokes stronger domain-wall pinning while also predicting easier rapid moment reorientation and lower hysteresis. No explanation is provided for how increased pinning avoids impeding wall motion or increasing coercivity.
